To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) human chorionic gonadotropin-producing bacteria are not a new species, (2) they are found in the blood, urine and feces of patients with overt cancer, (3) they are not found in the blood of normal individuals or in the urine or feces of patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy and (4) they are found to be associated with a variety of unusual morphological alterations of the bacterial cell walls, cytoplasm and cell division.

(1) hcg-producing bacteria are not a new or unique species as originally claimed; (2) the bacterial protein has close resemblance to the human trophic hormone; and (3) there is a possible association of hCG-like factor with the pathogenesis of cancer.

1) the hCG-like material in bacteria isolated from patients is not a unique species, but rather is expressed in bacteria of different morphological species, and 2) the hCG-producing bacteria share common morphological characteristics with the hCG-producing trophoblasts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery and characterization of a new group of microorganisms, which we have called the hCG-producing bacteria.
the isolation and characterization of bacteria from the urine, blood and sputum of patients with cancer.
the identification of a new class of human pathogens, the hCG-producing bacteria, and with the elucidation of their possible role in the pathogenesis of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hCG-producing bacteria do exist and that their expression of hCG and its individual subunits or fragments may be a consequence of the presence of hCG in patients' serum and/or urine.

hCG-like material is expressed in bacteria, and that this expression can be demonstrated by the use of monoclonal and/or polyclonal antibodies, but it does not necessarily imply that these bacteria are responsible for the elevated hCG levels found in cancer patients.
the hCG-like material expressed in bacteria of different genera is an antigenically and immunologically related but not identical protein to hCG.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bacteria isolated from the patients with cancer and the bacteria isolated from pregnant women were the same species and were identified as Streptoccocus faecalis.

we have shown that the bacteria that produce the hormone are not a new species but rather a number of different bacterial species, and that the hormone is produced by the bacteria as an adaptation to their environment, and not as a means to cause cancer.

hCG-like material was detected by immunocytochemical methods in 9 bacterial strains of 7 species, including two CWD variants and a Gram-positive Corynnebacterium that was Gram-negative during the time it expressed the hCG material, but was Gram-positive when the hCG material was not expressed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hCG-producing bacterial strains isolated from patients with malignancies are not a new species as claimed by other investigators.

the hCG-like material in the bacterial cells is not produced by a new and unique bacterium as claimed by others but by bacteria of different species that may or may not express the hCG-like protein under certain conditions.
the bacteria that we isolated are not unique to cancer.
